newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Will anyone vote "against" Halifax Plc?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Will anyone vote "against" Halifax Plc?.

text.p: The biggest share flotation ever on the London Stock Exchange is set to take Britain by storm this summer but not before a battle has been fought.

More than eight million members have been asked to vote on the flotation of the Halifax Building Society -- a mortgage lender and savings institution owned by its borrowing and saving members -- valued at around 12.0 billion pounds ($19.24 billion).
But many members think they would be better off if the Halifax kept its mutual status -- as a society owned by the people who use it -- rather than converting to a public company.
"They're being bribed with their own money," Serge Lourie, co-founder of the Halifax Action Group which is campaigning for members to vote against the flotation, told Reuters.

Each qualifying Halifax member would gain a minimum of 200 shares if the venture is approved. This would equal around 1,000 pounds ($1,600) on the basis of an estimate made by Halifax's bankers, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, in December.
Lourie said the share offer was a ploy by the Halifax board of directors to earn them handsome share options but from which most members would gain little in the long-run.
"I think the Halifax members would be far better off if it remained a mutual. We'd get better rates of interest and better mortgage rates," Lourie said.
PROPOSED FLOTATION DWARFS OTHER SHARE OFFERINGS
The Halifax flotation would dwarf the previous biggest share offering of 1.3 billion shares sold in British Telecom in 1993 worth a total of 5.33 billion pounds.

Lourie said that as a public company, the Halifax would be opened up to short-term pressures from outside shareholders expecting healthy dividends. These would be financed through higher mortgage interest rates and lower savings rates, he said.
Rob Thomas, building societies analyst at UBS, agreed:

"It's inevitable that their rates of interest will have to get worse because they've got to finance the dividend. In the case of the Abbey (National) that worked out at about a 1/3 of a percent," he said.

The Abbey National, floated in 1989, is the only building society to have become a public company to date, although the Woolwich, the Alliance & Leicester and the Northern Rock all plan to float in 1997 along with the Halifax.

But Thomas said the cash members received from the dividend would cancel out any loss of value from interest rates. The Halifax went one step further -- they said market forces would force them to give their members a good deal, or else.
"If we don't pay the right rates of interest, we'll lose business. It's a tough market out there," said Halifax general manager David Gilchrist.
The cost of mailing the transfer documents and advertising the vote will cost 153 million pounds, the Halifax said.
HALIFAX SETS NEW GOALS

Gilchrist said the flotation would unlock the society's capital and release its value to the shareholders. The Halifax would also have access to more capital with which to develop a broader range of financial services, he said.
"We're moving to be much more of a wide-ranging personal financial services business."

A 50 percent vote in favour of the flotation is needed for it to go ahead -- a higher proportion than the Abbey National required. This is so the Halifax does not have to put aside reserve assets under the terms of British legislation and can free more capital for investment.
NOT EVERYONE FOLLOWING THE TREND
Other building societies have decided their members' interests are best served if they stay as mutuals.
"We believe it is in the long-term interests of our customers that we stay as a building society," said a spokesman for Nationwide Building Society.
He said Nationwide's mutual status had enabled it to offer savings rates on average 3/4 percent above its main British competitors and mortgage rates around 1/4 percent lower.
"Over a lifetime that's an awful lot more than a one-off windfall payment they (Halifax members) will get on conversion."
He dismissed the idea that any loss of interest would be compensated for through dividend payments.
"They will get dividends but those dividends won't necessarily add up to the sort of value they would have got from a building society."
The Halifax's future will be determined when the votes are counted at a special general meeting on February 24. If the members vote in favour, the flotation will go ahead in June.
EACH TO THEIR OWN

UBS analyst Thomas said building societies were undergoing a polarisation, with the larger players seizing the opportunity to expand and gain access to new markets while medium sized societies specialised.
"I think that the Halifax's strategy for an organisation of that size is sensible but there is a place for these small niche players providing one or two services very cheaply and very well."
Lourie has claimed significant support for his fight to prevent the Halifax flotation though he admitted, "it's a case of David against Goliath".
The cash windfall would prove irresistible for most voters and sway them from the vote against, Thomas said, even if that meant sacrificing long-term gains from better interest rates.
"Most people are hard up and they want the shares." ($1=.6237 Pound)
